title: Why Common Tests Matter, Plus a Tribute to Dolly Parton
author: Chad Aldeman
summary: Chad Aldeman defends Iowa's requirement that private-school-choice participants take the same state standardized tests as public-school students, arguing common assessments serve five distinct audiences that a patchwork of school-chosen tests cannot. Beyond simply flagging which individual students are struggling, he argues common tests create a shared "on grade level" standard across schools and classrooms, give teachers an external check against grade inflation, let taxpayers evaluate whether publicly funded choice programs actually work, and let prospective parents compare schools using something more reliable than the self-selected 0.1 percent of parents who leave online reviews. He cites a Walton-funded RAND study concluding that nationally normed tests specifically cannot be compared across education-savings-account and public-school populations, undercutting the argument that any assessment is an adequate substitute for a common one. The piece closes with an unrelated tribute to Dolly Parton, crediting her Buddy Program with cutting local dropout rates from 35 to 6 percent and her Imagination Library with mailing over 300 million free books to children since 1995.
points: Argues common state tests serve five distinct audiences, students, teachers, parents, taxpayers, and school-choosing families, each of which a patchwork of school-selected nationally normed tests fails to serve equally well.

Cites a Walton Family Foundation-funded RAND study concluding that nationally normed assessment scores 'cannot be compared across ESA and non-ESA student populations' to evaluate whether school-choice participation causally affects achievement.
